title: Stasimon 2 (lines 881–921)

teacherSummary.text: The Chorus prays for reverence in word and deed and warns that insolence (hubris) breeds the tyrant. They fear that if oracles fail, religion itself is failing.

vocabulary.definition: overfed; having too much of something
vocabulary.context:
Of insolence is bred
The tyrant; insolence full blown,
With empty riches surfeited,
Scales the precipitous height and grasps the throne.
vocabulary.source: Liber et Libri contextual definition, hand-written against the line in Oedipus Rex

etymology.checked: 2026-10-21 (language, form and meaning taken from the Wiktionary entry's etymology templates; wording ours)

context.history: "Tyrant" (Greek tyrannos) first meant a ruler who took power by his own means, not necessarily a cruel one; the word's meaning darkened over time (Online Etymology Dictionary, n.d.-e).

significance: The ode turns from the plot to a general law of pride and fall, and raises the question of whether the gods' words still hold.
discussionQuestions: What is the difference between confidence and arrogance?
Where does theme appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with knowledge and blindness?

My lot be still to lead
The life of innocence and fly
Irreverence in word or deed,
To follow still those laws ordained on high
Whose birthplace is the bright ethereal sky.
No mortal birth they own,
Olympus their progenitor alone:
Ne’er shall they slumber in oblivion cold,
The god in them is strong and grows not old.
Of insolence is bred
The tyrant; insolence full blown,
With empty riches surfeited,
Scales the precipitous height and grasps the throne.
Then topples o’er and lies in ruin prone;
No foothold on that dizzy steep.
But O may Heaven the true patriot keep
Who burns with emulous zeal to serve the State.
God is my help and hope, on him I wait.

But the proud sinner, or in word or deed,
That will not Justice heed,
Nor reverence the shrine
Of images divine,
Perdition seize his vain imaginings,
If, urged by greed profane,
He grasps at ill-got gain,
And lays an impious hand on holiest things.
Who when such deeds are done
Can hope heaven’s bolts to shun?
If sin like this to honor can aspire,
Why dance I still and lead the sacred choir?
No more I’ll seek earth’s central oracle,
Or Abae’s hallowed cell,
Nor to Olympia bring
My votive offering.
If before all God’s truth be not bade plain.
O Zeus, reveal thy might,
King, if thou’rt named aright
Omnipotent, all-seeing, as of old;
For Laius is forgot;
His weird, men heed it not;
Apollo is forsook and faith grows cold.

literaryElements.label: Theme
literaryElements.explanation: The ode sets out a general law: arrogance, swollen with wealth, climbs to the top and then falls, while reverence in word and deed keeps a person safe.

literaryElements.label: Diction / vocabulary
literaryElements.explanation: The ode's key word is "insolence" (Storr's word for the Greek hybris), set against "reverence" and "innocence", so the vocabulary itself sorts people into the proud and the humble.

literaryElements.label: Tone / mood
literaryElements.explanation: The tone is solemn and anxious: the elders state rules about pride and the gods but end in fear that the oracles, and religion itself, may be failing.

themesAndDevelopment.development: The Chorus states the pattern of pride and fall as a law of the world and asks whether the gods still punish those who break it.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: the precipitous height
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: The steep height that insolence climbs stands for overreaching power, from which the only way is down.

weDoAnswers: "Tyrant" (Greek tyrannos) first meant a ruler who took power by his own means, not necessarily a cruel one; the word's meaning darkened over time (Online Etymology Dictionary, n.d.-e). Read closely: “Who when such deeds are done Can hope heaven’s bolts to shun?” (Chorus, lines 907–908).
analysis.weDoWords: “Deeds”, “heaven’s bolts” and “shun” stand out. The thunderbolts stand for the gods' punishment, and the question implies that no wrongdoer should escape it, so the elders are demanding that the gods act.

items.text: Does the play show Oedipus as guilty of hubris? Use this ode and one other scene.
items.lookFor: A case can be made that he is. The ode says "Of insolence is bred / The tyrant" and pictures insolence climbing "the precipitous height" (lines 890–893). Oedipus's treatment of Teiresias and Creon in the earlier episodes, accusing both of a plot without proof, fits that warning. Against this, he acts for the city and seeks the truth, so a strong answer weighs pride against public duty.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?

items.text: Is the Chorus's threat to stop worshipping at the oracles an act of faith or of doubt? Argue with evidence.
items.lookFor: It is an act of anxious faith. The elders say they will no longer seek "earth's central oracle" or bring offerings to Olympia (lines 911–914) if the god's truth is not made plain. Yet they end by praying, "O Zeus, reveal thy might" (line 916), which means they still expect the god to answer. Their threat shows how much they need the oracles to be true. A strong answer weighs the doubt in the threat against the hope in the prayer.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

items.text: Which matters more to the Chorus in Stasimon 2: the safety of Thebes or the honour of the gods? Argue with evidence.
items.lookFor: The honour of the gods matters more. The ode prays for the "true patriot" who serves the State (lines 896–897), but most of it defends the "laws ordained on high" (line 884) and fears that "Apollo is forsook and faith grows cold" (line 921). The elders even ask, "Why dance I still and lead the sacred choir?" (line 910). A strong answer may argue that for the Chorus the two cannot be separated, since a city without reverence cannot be safe.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
